speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Health following the error in the Khoo Teck Puat Hospital laboratory test for cancer patients (a) how many patients suffered side effects arising from being given the wrong treatment; (b) how many were treated at private hospitals versus Government hospitals; and (c) what is the average cost of medication incurred by all these patients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Health with regard to the case of breast cancer patients at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital who may have received unnecessary treatment since 2012 due to inaccurate test results (a) what are the key revelations from the review of the process; (b) what measures have been implemented to prevent similar incidents; and (c) whether there have been cases of patients suffering from detrimental effects.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Health with regard to cancers inaccurately classified HER2-positive by Khoo Teck Puat Hospital laboratory (a) how many patients (i) received unnecessary treatment and (ii) suffered significant or long-term side effects thereby; (b) what is the ensuing cost to affected patients; (c) what is being done to help these patients; and (d) what measures are taken to ensure fidelity of laboratory tests.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Health with regard to the incident at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital where breast cancer patients received unnecessary treatment since 2012 (a) why did subsequent follow-up checks on the patients over the years not pick up any misdiagnosis from the earlier test; and (b) whether there are regular audits of hospitals and medical clinics on laboratory protocols to identify lapses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: asked the Minister for Health what are the reasons for the wrong test results for cancer patients at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital and what measures will be put in place to ensure that such errors do not occur again.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Preliminary investigations by the laboratory suggested that some of the HER2 results may be inaccurate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Following the incident, MOH has been working closely with KTPH to ensure that affected patients are provided with adequate support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH has sent the samples of all patients, who have been tested HER2 positive since 2012, when HER2 testing first started in KTPH, to external laboratories for re-testing to determine how many have received inaccurate results.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Preliminary investigations by the KTPH laboratory suggest that the inaccurate results could be due to a suboptimal staining process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The KTPH laboratory has since stopped in-house testing of HER2.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH has also issued an alert to our other public healthcare institutions to conduct a quick review of their laboratory-developed IHC tests to ensure that positivity rates are within the acceptable range.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thus far, we have not received any reports of similar risks from other healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH's Department of Laboratory Medicine is subject to regular inspection by MOH as part of regulatory processes under the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics (PHMC) Act to ensure that its laboratory facilities, systems and processes are in place to meet patient and personnel safety standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, the laboratory is accredited by the College of American Pathologists (CAP), where the last biennial inspections by peers were conducted in 2019.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Joint care teams have been formed, comprising KTPH surgeons, histopathologists and the treating oncologists, to review the individual care plans for these affected patients, based on the change in their HER2 status.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH and the treating oncologists are in the process of actively reaching out to these patients to conduct open disclosure and assess these patients for any potential side effects due to unnecessary treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The more common side effects include diarrhoea, chills and fatigue – these are usually short-lasting.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH is also reviewing the bills of these affected patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH is also ready to provide any clinical and financial support to the affected patients including on-going or follow-on treatments, if any, which may be needed as a result of this over-treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The National Healthcare Group has convened an independent review committee, comprising external experts from multiple relevant disciplines in the healthcare industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The objective is to conduct a thorough evaluation of the incident, to understand better the lapses that have occurred and recommend appropriate measures to improve the process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This ensures that any system gaps are identified and addressed swiftly to prevent recurrence of similar incidents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The committee's investigations are on-going right now and more time would be required to ensure a thorough review.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: NHG will provide an update when more information is available and these findings will be shared with the other healthcare institutions for improvement.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have also raised this issue with me, in my Member of Parliament capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it has, and it is incumbent upon the authorities and the hospital to do the very best to support the affected patients in as holistic a way as possible and as compassionately as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if there has been an issue with the charts for whatever reason, it is, of course, a concern for navigating the patient care journey and giving the relevant treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, I must say that Herceptin treatment for HER2 positive patients usually is not so much of a monotherapy, that means on a standalone basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Usually, it is in combination with other chemotherapy drugs for breast cancer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in other words, even in a HER2 negative patient, where you do not need Herceptin treatment, you will still require some chemotherapy to overcome breast cancer, and therefore, you will still have to come for recurrent visits, treatment, monitoring and testing by the managing oncologist.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But we know that some of these can create a lot more anxiety, maybe a few extra visits that will be required for monitoring of side effects.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: KTPH and the managing oncologists and doctors will take a compassionate approach to reassure, to also help these patients to overcome their disease and anxieties by keeping close communication with them through a more dedicated care team, especially those who are affected by the change in result status.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I must also say that in this situation where the issue is more of a false positive, it does mean that some patients would have perhaps, over treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think it is probably a preferred state than to have under treatment, especially when you have cancer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this situation, HER2 testing has shown that some of them should have been classified as HER2 negative, meaning that actually the patient does have a better prognosis compared to those who are HER2 positive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Overall, it is not necessarily a bad thing for the patients to be actually reclassified as HER2 negative on testing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think that will go in some way to relieve some of the financial pressures and stresses that a patient has undergone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the second question of whether other immunohistochemistry tests would be reviewed; I think we must understand that immunohistochemistry testing is classified in most laboratories as a highly complex test.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By highly complex, what I mean is that it is a test that is not quite the same as you drawing a blood test – pop it into the machine and the result comes up within a few minutes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is a multi-step process that has multiple steps of human intervention in the process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, as a tumour specimen is removed, what we call cold ischemic time – how soon the tumour, after it is removed from the body – gets put into a fixation, that means to fix the tissue in the chemical, usually it is recommended to be less than one hour.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, how the operating team in the Operating Theatre, not even the pathologist, just how the operating team handles the tissue – when do they take a specimen out, when do they call for the team to put into the solution; you must also put into the correct solution, otherwise if you put in the wrong chemical to fix the tumour tissue, that sample cannot be used for IHC staining.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Then, when it goes to the laboratory, how thick the specimen is sliced, what kind of stains are used, what kind of temperature that is done, what is the concentration of the stains being used, what is the choice of antibody and subsequently after staining, how the pathologists themselves grade the degree of staining.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And the degree of grading or staining is what we call a semi quantitative method.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It means it is not a "plus" or "minus", "yes" or "no".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is a gradation of degrees of staining just like when you look at your iPhone photos, and you try to adjust the contrast.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Between two sets of persons looking at the adjustment, to you, this may look pleasing enough, dark enough, but to another person, this may be too light.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there is some degree of inter-observer variation which trained pathologists must then make the judgement call and say is this dark enough stain to be deemed as a positive 3+, 2+, 1+ or 0.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, you can appreciate that this being a very complex test, as in most other immunohistochemistry tests, will require multiple levels of validation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I will also say that the reason why this issue was discovered is because the institutional processes within KTPH have allowed this to be picked up.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will also use this chance to learn about some of the failures that may have happened in this multi-step process and help the laboratory to strengthen them for other immunohistochemistry tests as well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Actually, the main thing around it is this, because as the Senior Minister of State has said, all these patients had gone for recurrent visits to their respective doctors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think that is the key to the issue.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is going to be a little bit technical but let me attempt to explain this in a way that most people can understand.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Inherent in any laboratory test, there is always a chance of false positivity, false negativity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That relates to the sensitivity and specificity of the test.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In recent months, because of COVID-19, we have all been doing PCR testing, everybody is a little bit more attuned to the concept of why a certain test can give you a false positive and false negative result.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Immunohistochemistry test actually is fairly notorious for having this kind of risk because, as I said, it is semi-quantitative, so the staining process is like mixing poster colours.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If any part of the mixing process – the process of processing the specimen by putting stains, dyes and counter-stains – is not done optimally, the key word here is "optimal", you can perform all the steps but if the timing is a bit off, maybe the concentration is off by a little bit, the kind of picture that comes out on the slide that the pathologist gets to look at, will be quite different in terms of contrast and stain.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: What we need to do, as in this instance, where the clinical practice within an institution does regular review of data accumulated over time; because to show that there is now an over-representation over time, you need to have accumulated enough caseload over a period of time, to show on a retrospective basis that after three years, five years, I accumulated 200 patients, 1,000 patients, and I aggregate the data and I realise, "Oops, it is actually more than 6%".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Then, this is when it triggers a review.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But when you first start the test, you only have one case, two cases, three cases, there is not enough to do statistical analysis to tell you whether you are above or below the 6% mark.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I hope that gives a sense that it is not a complete failure of the system; it is inherent in the test and that is how a review process through a multi-disciplinary tumour board picks up any outlier conclusions to trigger a review.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it a standard timeframe for enough statistics to flag up a possible error?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The last supplementary question is about compensation to the victims.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What sort of compensation is being considered and is a lifetime of free healthcare on the cards?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When I said in my reply that KTPH is reviewing all the results from 2012, 2012 was taken at a point in which the test first started in KTPH.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It does not mean that all the results going back to 2012 are erroneous.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in that sense, KTPH is being prudent and careful, super kiasu, going back all the way to when the test first started.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It may well be that the errors could have occurred in the last three months or six months.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think the key point usually is when the reagent has been changed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A different brand of reagent or a different provider of the reagent could usually be the starting point of why the protocol or the test conditions were no longer as optimal as they should be.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But going back to 2012 when the test first started was really trying to be comprehensive and to be careful, to make sure that we do not miss anybody in the process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It does not mean that the test was erroneous from 2012.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The results of the review are still on-going, so I do not want to prejudge the review process from the experts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Let us wait for the experts to look at all the results going back to 2012 and then decide at which point, what step of the process that could have been where the error occurred.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But to then say that this translates to a lifetime of compensation, I think that would be a little bit too far a thing to stretch because most of the complications, if any, or most of the side effects relating to the treatment, are transient – diarrhoea, a bit of fever, a bit of chills.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They do not have long-term consequences, they are not long-lasting and we have to take that in the correct context of medical treatment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I also had a question about a second independent test for serious illnesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I take that as a general question which in any form of medical diagnostics, if the clinician is unsure that a particular test alone cannot give you a high degree of probability of predicting a positive diagnosis or presence of an illness, then it behoves clinical judgement to call for a second test.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It does not necessarily mean that an alternative is available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Although in the literature, there are other alternative tests that could be done but we have to consider that against the time needed to do it because that could delay treatment, and also whether that brings on unnecessary costs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That, I think, we should leave it to the experts to come up with the process guidelines on what is a testing algorithm to decide for 	Herceptin-related treatment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think the Senior Minister of State also have not fully answered my Parliamentary Question regarding, how many patients were actually involved and how many patients have MOH engaged in the first place currently now that are affected by this particular error.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, what measures have been taken to ensure the well-being of the patients, both psychologically as well as physical health?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to know what was the average cost of the medication, of this particular medicine that was just mentioned.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Because the Senior Minister of State did not mention anything about the costs; he just mentioned that it will be refunded but I am not sure what is the actual cost.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I do have a patient, who is my resident in Sembawang GRC, who saw me at my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: She was very worried when she saw the news; she said she is one of them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When I asked her whether has MOH contacted her, she said not yet.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, she was asking me what legal help can she now seek.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State what avenues do affected patients have to seek compensation for such an error?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, it needs the managing oncologists to go on a one-to-one with any of these patients whose status have been reclassified, to do a detailed conversation on their own clinical prognosis, what is the stage of the tumour, what treatment has already been given in the past, what will be the on-going treatment needed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Not all patients, I must say, who have been tested HER2 positive be it now or previously, will go on to Herceptin treatment because it is a treatment decision that is guided by the needs of the patient, not just by the test alone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are some patients for which the body may be too frail; even if you are HER2 positive, you may not receive Herceptin treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the other hand, there are recurrent tumours where the oncologist feels that you have reached end of line, you will still require Herceptin treatment as a last resort, even though it may not be the first line in some other cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The decision matrix is not a straightforward one.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For patients who may be affected, it is best to seek your oncologist's advice.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if you have not been contacted specifically for this, it means that you are okay, your status remains as it was from the last conversation with your oncologist.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I do not have the exact numbers right now because it also depends on how many doses, how long the duration of treatment each patient got, and also different body size of patients may require different dosages to begin with.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is something that we cannot generalise; it is probably quite individual.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why the dedicated care team from KTPH, especially the oncologists, will have to reach out to affected patients one by one and go through the conversation in a detailed manner.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to the physical side effects that many of these patients might have suffered, some of them might suffer panic attacks, anxiety attacks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, would Khoo Teck Puat Hospital be able to support medical costs relating to mental health?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A panic attack or anxiety episode can occur with or without cancer, can occur with or without treatment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There can be a myriad of factors involved.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But the joint care team will deal with the patients with compassion and find a way to help them overcome this current hurdle they are facing.
